title: Setup Instructions for Students
text:
Follow these steps to set up and publish your research website.


Before you begin, make sure you have the following:

A GitHub account (free at github.com)
GitHub Desktop installed on your computer
R and RStudio







Click the “Use this template” button.
Select Create a new repository.
Use the Owner dropdown menu to select your github user
Name the repository. This will be in your web address! Choose something professional like your name.
Click Create repository from template.
You should now have this newly created repository on your own GitHub.





On your computer: Make sure the GitHub Desktop is open.
On GitHub: In your own repository on GitHub, Click the “<> Code” button.
Select Open with GitHub Desktop.
Choose a local path for the placement of the directory (not a cloud service). For example: (/Users/YourUserame/GitHub/introR2026)
Select Clone.





[!IMPORTANT] 1. Open RStudio 2. Create a new Rproj file in the existing local directory of your repository 3. Open .Rproj file 4. Edit the following files in RStudio




Replace “Your Name” with your name.
Update the About Me section.
Add your research interests.
Replace “your photo.jpg” with the filename of a photo of yourself & by adding the photo to the directory.
Update places that say “link” with the correct internet link or email address, if desired.





Update the descriptions of your projects.
Add links to additional projects as you create them.





Change the title to your project title.
Write your final report.
Replace all placeholder text with your own content.




styles.css * Customize colors, fonts, and other styling options if desired.
_quarto.yml * add new links to the navbar
README.md * This is a place to add information to the GitHub reponsitory, but will not be displayed on your rendered website.
.gitignore * List files here you don’t want synced to GitHub. For example, if you want to keep your data.csv files local and not online list them here
SETUP.md * These are instructions to create this site. No need to modify this file.




In RStudio, you can preview your website before publishing.
Run the following command in the RStudio Terminal:
quarto preview
To render the website before pushing your changes, run:
quarto render



When you are satisfied with your changes:

Open GitHub Desktop.
Review the files you modified.
Enter a commit summary and an optional description.
Click Commit to main.
Click Push origin to upload your changes to GitHub.





Go to your repository on GitHub.
Click Settings.
Select Pages from the left sidebar.
Under Build and deployment:

Source: Select Deploy from a branch.
Branch: Select main.
Folder: Select /docs.

Click Save.





Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub to deploy your site.
Return to Settings → Pages.
You should see a URL similar to:
https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY/
Click the link to view your website.





Whenever you want to update your website:

Edit your .qmd files.
Commit and push your changes using GitHub Desktop.
Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to rebuild your site.
Refresh your browser to view the updated website.




If your website is not updating:

Go to your GitHub repository.
Click the Actions tab.
Open the most recent workflow run.
Review any error messages if the build failed.







Go to Settings → Pages.
Confirm that:

The branch is set to main.
The folder is set to /docs.

Your website URL should appear on this page after deployment.




Always use forward slashes (/) in links, even when using Windows.
# Correct
[Link](projects/final-report.qmd)

# Incorrect
[Link](projects\final-report.qmd)




To add another page, such as a poster, publication, or additional project:

Create a new .qmd file in the projects/ folder.
Edit projects.qmd and add a link to the new page.
Commit and push your changes.
Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to update your website.





Quarto Documentation
GitHub Pages Documentation
Markdown Guide
Git Basics


Need help? Contact your instructor or refer to the resources listed above.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Maternal health risk assessment is important for identifying pregnant women who may require additional medical care. In this project, I analyzed a maternal health risk dataset collected from hospitals and community clinics in rural Bangladesh. The dataset includes maternal age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, heart rate, and maternal risk level.
I used R to compare low-, mid-, and high-risk groups, examine relationships among the clinical measurements, and determine whether principal component analysis revealed patterns among the maternal risk categories.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Maternal health risk assessment is important for identifying pregnant women who may require additional medical care. In this project, I analyzed a maternal health risk dataset collected from hospitals and community clinics in rural Bangladesh. The dataset includes maternal age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, heart rate, and maternal risk level.
I used R to compare low-, mid-, and high-risk groups, examine relationships among the clinical measurements, and determine whether principal component analysis revealed patterns among the maternal risk categories.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Packages Used

library(tidyverse)
library(here)

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Get the Data

maternal_data <- read_csv(
  here("data", "Maternal Health Risk Data Set.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Prepare the Data

maternal_data <- maternal_data |>
  mutate(
    RiskLevel = str_to_lower(str_trim(RiskLevel)),
    RiskLevel = factor(
      RiskLevel,
      levels = c("low risk", "mid risk", "high risk"),
      ordered = TRUE))


levels(maternal_data$RiskLevel)

[1] "low risk"  "mid risk"  "high risk"

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Questions

1. How many observations are classified as low, mid, or high risk?
To describe the distribution of maternal risk, I counted the number of observations in each risk category.

maternal_data |>
  count(RiskLevel, sort = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = n,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n),
    vjust = -0.4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Observations in Each Maternal Risk Category",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Number of Observations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Low risk was the most common category, with 406 observations (40.0%), followed by mid risk with 336 observations (33.1%) and high risk with 272 observations (26.8%). Thus, more than one-quarter of the dataset was classified as high risk.


2. How does maternal age differ across risk groups?
Next, I examined how maternal age varied across the low-, mid-, and high-risk categories.

maternal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = Age,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Maternal Age Across Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The high-risk group had the highest median maternal age, while the low-risk group had the lowest. Although the distributions overlapped, older observations were more common in the high-risk category.


3. How do systolic and diastolic blood pressure differ across risk groups?
I then compared systolic and diastolic blood pressure across the three maternal risk categories.

maternal_data |>
  select(RiskLevel, SystolicBP, DiastolicBP) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(SystolicBP, DiastolicBP),
    names_to = "BloodPressureType",
    values_to = "BloodPressure"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = BloodPressure,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~BloodPressureType,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Blood Pressure Across Maternal Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Blood Pressure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Both systolic and diastolic blood pressure were higher in the high-risk group than in the low- and mid-risk groups. The separation was especially noticeable for diastolic blood pressure.


4. How does blood sugar differ across maternal risk groups?
Blood sugar distributions were evaluated across the low-, mid-, and high-risk groups.

maternal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = BS,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Blood Sugar Across Maternal Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Blood Sugar"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Blood sugar was clearly higher in the high-risk group, with a median of approximately 11 compared with about 7 in the low- and mid-risk groups. The high-risk group also showed greater variability.


5. How do body temperature and heart rate differ across risk groups?
To assess additional vital signs, I compared body temperature and heart rate among the maternal risk categories.

maternal_data |>
  select(RiskLevel, BodyTemp, HeartRate) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(BodyTemp, HeartRate),
    names_to = "Measurement",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = RiskLevel,
    y = Value,
    fill = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~Measurement,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body Temperature and Heart Rate Across Risk Categories",
    x = "Maternal Risk Level",
    y = "Observed Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Body temperature was generally similar across the three groups, although the mid- and high-risk groups showed a wider range. Heart rate was slightly higher in the high-risk group, and one unusually low value appeared in the low-risk group.


6. Which clinical measurements are most strongly associated with maternal risk level?
To identify the measurements most strongly associated with maternal risk, I converted the ordered risk categories to numeric scores: low risk as 1, mid risk as 2, and high risk as 3. I then calculated Spearman correlations.

risk_associations <- maternal_data |>
  mutate(
    RiskScore = as.numeric(RiskLevel)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(
        Age,
        SystolicBP,
        DiastolicBP,
        BS,
        BodyTemp,
        HeartRate
      ),
      ~cor(
        .x,
        RiskScore,
        method = "spearman",
        use = "complete.obs"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Measurement",
    values_to = "Correlation"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Correlation))

risk_associations

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  Measurement Correlation
  <chr>             <dbl>
1 BS                0.445
2 SystolicBP        0.398
3 DiastolicBP       0.319
4 Age               0.289
5 HeartRate         0.186
6 BodyTemp          0.167



risk_associations |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = reorder(Measurement, Correlation),
    y = Correlation
  )) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Clinical Measurements Associated With Maternal Risk Level",
    x = "Clinical Measurement",
    y = "Spearman Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Blood sugar had the strongest positive correlation with increasing maternal risk level, followed by systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and age. Heart rate and body temperature showed much weaker relationships.


7. Can PCA visually separate observations according to maternal risk category?
Finally, I performed principal component analysis using the six numeric clinical measurements. The variables were centered and standardized because they were measured on different scales.

# Create the PCA model
pca_model <- maternal_data |>
  select(
    Age,
    SystolicBP,
    DiastolicBP,
    BS,
    BodyTemp,
    HeartRate
  ) |>
  prcomp(
    center = TRUE,
    scale. = TRUE
  )

# Calculate variance explained
pca_variance <- pca_model$sdev^2 / sum(pca_model$sdev^2)

pc1_percent <- round(pca_variance[1] * 100, 1)
pc2_percent <- round(pca_variance[2] * 100, 1)

# Create PCA scores
pca_data <- as_tibble(pca_model$x) |>
  mutate(
    RiskLevel = maternal_data$RiskLevel
  )

# Create the PCA plot
pca_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    color = RiskLevel
  )) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA of Maternal Health Measurements",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "PC1 and PC2 explain ",
      round(pc1_percent + pc2_percent, 1),
      "% of the total variation"
    ),
    x = paste0(
      "Principal Component 1 (",
      pc1_percent,
      "%)"
    ),
    y = paste0(
      "Principal Component 2 (",
      pc2_percent,
      "%)"
    ),
    color = "Risk Level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The PCA plot shows partial separation of the maternal risk categories. High-risk observations were more frequently located on the positive side of Principal Component 1, while many low- and mid-risk observations were concentrated near the center or negative side. However, substantial overlap remained among all three groups, indicating that the six clinical measurements did not completely separate patients by maternal risk category. One low-risk observation appeared far from the other points along Principal Component 2 and may represent an unusual record or outlier.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Discussion
High-risk observations generally had higher age, blood pressure, and blood sugar. Blood sugar showed the strongest association with risk level, while body temperature and heart rate showed weaker differences. PCA showed partial separation among risk groups, but considerable overlap remained.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh
text:
Conclusions
Maternal risk level was most strongly associated with blood sugar and blood pressure. These results show associations only and do not prove causation.

title: Exploratory Analysis of Maternal Health Risk Factors in Bangladesh Using R
text:
My final project for CELL 6351 - Intro to Reproducible Data Analysis Using R.
I will analyze a maternal health risk dataset collected from hospitals and community clinics in rural Bangladesh. The dataset includes age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, heart rate, and maternal risk level. Using R and the tidyverse package, I will summarize and visualize differences among low-, mid-, and high-risk groups through bar charts, boxplots, scatterplots, and dimension-reduction methods such as PCA or UMAP. I will examine the number of patients in each risk category, differences in age, blood pressure, and blood sugar across risk groups, the clinical measurements most strongly associated with risk level, and whether PCA or UMAP can separate patients according to risk category. I will present the final analysis as a reproducible Quarto webpage containing the R code, figures, interpretations, and conclusion.
